issues: Wrong year for the competition. Both Census Bureau web pages (and IBM's history page) say it was '1888', but the Census Bureau's own book-length history puts the test in 1889: Truesdell, The Development of Punch Card Tabulation in the Bureau of the Census 1890–1940 (1965), pp. 40–41. There, Superintendent Robert P. Porter (in office from 1889) named the committee at the suggestion of the Secretary of the Interior 'in 1889', and its report on the St. Louis test is dated November 30, 1889. The January 2016 Census page is also internally unreliable: it says Hollerith filed his patent application in September 1888 'after his decisive win', but the application 'Art of Compiling Statistics' was filed in 1884.

The run-on sentence with two nested dashes hides the order of events, and 'after a 1911 merger it was renamed IBM' makes it sound as if the Tabulating Machine Company itself was renamed. In fact the 1911 merger created the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, and CTR was renamed IBM in 1924.
The numbers (72.5, 5.5, 144.5, 100.5 hours; nearly 63 million people; patent of 8 January 1889) are all confirmed.

fieldFixes.summary: In a test run for the Census Office in 1889, Herman Hollerith's punch-card system transcribed data from four St. Louis enumeration districts in 72.5 hours and tabulated it in 5.5 hours; his two rivals needed 144.5 and 100.5 hours just to transcribe. Hollerith, whose electro-mechanical tabulating machine had been patented on 8 January 1889, won the contract to supply tabulators for the 1890 census. Clerks punched each person's answers into cards that the machine read electrically, and census clerks tabulated data for nearly 63 million people this way. Hollerith founded the Tabulating Machine Company in 1896; a 1911 merger folded it into the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, which was renamed International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924.

issues: The title ('the first privacy statute') and significance ('The first privacy statute was a consent rule') overstate the case. Earlier statutes protected privacy interests, and this dataset records several of them: the U.S. Post Office Act of 1792 (opening letters), California's 1862 ban on tapping telegraph lines, and France's 1868 press-law offence of publishing 'a fact of private life'. What was new in 1903 was a statutory right of privacy in likeness and name.

issues: The summary's last sentence ('The same principle — no publication identifying any individual — was later codified') points back to a principle the summary never states. It also leaves out the 1929 act's main novelty, which its own source records: it was 'the first to extend the promise to individuals', i.e. 'No publication shall be made by the Census Office whereby the data furnished by any particular establishment or individual can be identified'.

The 'to the detriment of the person or persons to whom such information relates' wording is attributed by Ruggles & Magnuson to how 'the Census Bureau further clarified' the 1929 act. The 13 U.S.C. § 8 derivation notes (Cornell LII) trace the later 'detriment' proviso to the transcript section of the 1929 act (June 18, 1929, ch. 28, § 18, 46 Stat. 25), so it is narrower than a general bar. The corrected wording attributes the reading to the Bureau.

The 1954 Title 13 codification is confirmed by the Census Bureau's own 2001 monograph (added). The significance claim about wartime breach is supported by the same article (Second War Powers Act 1942; wartime disclosures documented by Seltzer and Anderson 2007).

fieldFixes.summary: Earlier census acts had required that census information “shall be used only for the statistical purposes for which it is supplied” (1909) and that only sworn census employees examine individual reports (the act for the 1920 census). The act providing for the Fifteenth Census, approved 18 June 1929, was the first census law to extend the no-identification promise to individuals: “No publication shall be made by the Census Office whereby the data furnished by any particular establishment or individual can be identified.” As the Census Bureau read it, the act also protected the information from being used “to the detriment of the person or persons to whom such information relates”. Congress codified the 1929 law in 1954 as Title 13 of the U.S. Code, which carries virtually the same language.
